notes.meaning: David attacked the Philistines and broke their control over Israel once and for all. He captured Metheg-ammah, which was their chief city Gath along with its nearby towns. By taking their main stronghold, David turned the tables on a long-time enemy and gave Israel lasting peace on its western border.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that rather than naming a specific town, Metheg-ammah means 'the bridle of the mother city' or stands as a figure of speech for total Philistine surrender.

notes.meaning: David defeated the army of Moab and made the captured soldiers lie down in rows on the ground. He used a measuring cord to mark off two lengths of men to be executed and one full length to be spared. The survivors became subjects of David and were required to pay regular taxes to Israel.

David marched north and defeated King Hadadezer of Zobah as that ruler moved to secure power near the Euphrates River. This victory extended Israel's reach all the way to the great river. It fulfilled the promise of land that God had made to Abraham centuries earlier.

David captured many chariots, horsemen, and foot soldiers from the army of Zobah. He crippled most of the horses by cutting their leg tendons so they could never be used in war again, keeping only enough for one hundred chariots. This showed that David trusted in the Lord rather than in military hardware, obeying God's law that kings should not multiply horses.

The Arameans from the city of Damascus came to help Hadadezer fight against Israel. David met them in battle and struck down twenty-two thousand of their men. Their alliance could not stop the king whom God was defending.

David placed military posts inside the territory of Damascus and forced the Arameans to pay regular tribute. The writer emphasizes that David's own strength was not the real reason for these great victories. The Lord protected David and gave him success wherever he went.

David took the valuable gold shields carried by Hadadezer's elite officers and brought them back to Jerusalem. Instead of keeping them for his own personal display, he set them aside as public trophies of God's victory. They stood as visible proof of the Lord's power over mighty pagan rulers.

David captured a vast amount of bronze from two cities that had belonged to Hadadezer. Years later, his son Solomon used this very metal to cast the great bronze basin and pillars for the temple of the Lord. God used the spoils of these battles to supply the future house of worship.

King Toi of Hamath learned that David had destroyed the entire army of Hadadezer, who had been Toi's bitter enemy. Toi sent his son Joram on an official royal visit to greet David and congratulate him on his victory. Joram brought valuable gifts made of silver, gold, and bronze to form a friendly alliance with Israel.

David dedicated all the costly gifts from Hamath directly to the Lord, along with the silver and gold taken from other conquered nations. These spoils came from Edom, Moab, Ammon, Philistia, Amalek, and Zobah. David placed this immense treasure into the sanctuary treasury so it could one day build the temple.

David won great fame when his army struck down eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, south of the Dead Sea. This victory broke the power of another persistent enemy of God's people. The Lord continued to fulfill his promise to make David's name great among the nations.

David placed military garrisons throughout Edom, bringing all the Edomites under his rule. This fulfilled the ancient word to Rebekah that the older brother would serve the younger brother. The writer repeats that the Lord was the true source of David's victory wherever he went.

David reigned over the entire united nation of Israel with fairness and integrity, giving equal justice to all his people. Foreign wars did not stop him from caring for his own citizens at home. In his righteous and peaceful rule, David served as a picture of the coming reign of Christ.

David set up a skilled group of leaders to help manage the nation. He placed Joab over the army as commander-in-chief, and appointed Jehoshaphat as the royal recorder to keep the official history and records of the kingdom.

Zadok and Ahimelech served as the chief priests, directing the public worship of the Lord. Seraiah was the royal scribe or secretary of state, managing government letters, official documents, and state laws.
Benaiah commanded the Cherethites and Pelethites, who formed the king's trusted personal bodyguard. David also gave important leadership duties in the royal administration to his own sons.

differ.view: Some evangelicals understand the title given to David's sons as chief ministers or royal administrators rather than religious priests, since God's law limited the priesthood to the family of Aaron and the tribe of Levi.
